$comment: GATE is the one menu item whose target is a prompt rather than a skill, and its prompt text says in so many
words not to merge the workflows it routes between. A reply that names GATE and then names a workflow behind it
has done the merge the item forbids, so the menu code alone cannot decide this one.
It is the case the workflow oracle exists for. Before that oracle was added the contracts could not see this
failure at all and only the replay harness caught it.
A frozen copy of one case of the live corpus, of the menu it is scored against, and of the user's message.
Those three plus the reply are the whole input to scoreCase, so all three are stored here rather than read
live: a replay has to keep scoring the scenario it was derived against after the corpus moves on, and
npm run test:eval-routing-data already holds the live corpus against the shipped menu.

expected.rationale: The ask is the order to run workflows in, not one workflow. GATE is the menu item that answers with a sequence, and it is a prompt rather than a skill, so expectedWorkflow is null and naming a workflow behind it is the merge its own prompt text forbids.

derivation: The action is route and the menu code is GATE, both as the oracle expects, so actionCorrect and menuCorrect are
true. The oracle expects a null workflow, because the menu maps GATE to a prompt and not to a skill, and the
reply names bmad-testarch-trace, so workflowCorrect is false and routeCorrect with it.
decidingTokens is [release gate, order] and the reason carries both. scopeTokens is [epic 7] and the scope
reads "epic 7", so scopeOk is true. Everything except the workflow is right, which is what makes this case a
test of that one rule rather than of the routing in general.

answer.reason: this is the release gate path and the order depends on which evidence you already have
